# Bayh–Dole, Reagan, and Valley Ideology {#sec-4-10}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1980–1990
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does a regional elite capture national policy?

**The answer.** By supplying the personnel and the argument. Reagan's economics
came substantially from an institution on Stanford's campus, and the Bayh-Dole
Act of the same year let universities patent federally funded research. One
statute turned public money into private licensing revenue, and one think tank
turned a regional politics into a national one.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, now written
into statute, and elite network reproduction operating at the level of national
policy. This is the chapter where the Hoover Institution's function, planted in
Act III ch. 5, finally pays off.

**The key fact.** Bayh-Dole allowed universities to take title to inventions
made with federal research funding. The public pays for the research; the
university patents the result; the licensee monopolises it. Act III ch. 11's
triangle acquired an intellectual property regime.

**The human anchor.** George Shultz and Milton Friedman, both at the Hoover
Institution, both routed into national power — the archive Hoover built in 1919
functioning exactly as an archive of power should.

**Excluded voices.** The taxpayer, whose research funding became private
licensing revenue without a corresponding return, and the industries and regions
that Reagan-era policy did not favour. Also the biotech patients on the
receiving end of the pricing that Genentech's model made possible.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that a regional elite captured national policy by
showing its economic programme, its personnel, and its institutional base all
originate in one corridor.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** A statute nobody has heard of that changed what a university is.
   Open on Bayh-Dole, not on Reagan.
2. **What Bayh-Dole did.** Title to federally funded inventions. The mechanics
   of technology licensing offices that follow.
3. **Stanford's licensing revenue.** Concrete: the Cohen-Boyer patents, and what
   they earned. Public research, private royalty stream.
4. **The Hoover Institution in 1980.** Friedman, Shultz, and the pipeline into
   the administration. Then look back at Act III ch. 5 and name the payoff
   explicitly.
5. **Capital gains and deregulation.** What changed and who benefited. Venture
   capital's growth across the early 1980s, sourced.
6. **Genentech's 1980 IPO.** Biology as an asset class. Recombinant DNA out of a
   Bay Area laboratory into a public offering; the Cohen-Boyer patent underneath
   it.
7. **Valley ideology assembled.** Meritocratic self-description plus
   deregulatory politics plus federal funding retained. Name the contradiction
   without sneering at it; it is held sincerely by most of the people holding
   it.
8. **The excluded.** Taxpayer return; drug pricing; regions outside the favoured
   corridor.
9. **Landing.** The pipeline now runs to Washington in both directions. Act V's
   inauguration platform is visible from here.
:::
